title: The Other Side of Bayes: Rethinking False Positives in Health Screening - TimmermanReport.com
gist: The author, long a screening skeptic, reverses toward cautious optimism: Bayes' theorem condemns single-shot screening of healthy people to overwhelming false positives, but the same theorem implies that accumulated individual context — serial imaging, longitudinal molecular baselines, complementary reflex tests — can progressively raise positive predictive value. Evidence cited includes an NYU prostate-cancer AI study where specificity rose from under 30% to over 90% at ~90% sensitivity as prior context was added, and a Göteborg-2 reflex-testing analysis that cut MRIs 41% with no AI at all.

themes.theme: The Bayesian trap in low-prevalence screening

insights.claim: Screening 10,000 apparently healthy people for a disease with 1-in-1,000 prevalence using a test that is 99% sensitive and 99% specific yields roughly 110 positives of which only about 10 are real, meaning about nine out of ten positive results are wrong.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: The arithmetic that caps the clinical value of any consumer screening product marketed on sensitivity/specificity alone; PPV, not accuracy, is the number to demand.
insights.quote: even with a test that is 99% sensitive and 99% specific, about nine out of ten positive results will be wrong
insights.locator: Imagine screening 10,000 apparently healthy people

insights.claim: Interpretation of any screening test depends not only on the test's intrinsic characteristics but on the pre-test probability that the person had the disease, so when that prior probability is very low even an excellent test delivers misleading results.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Explains why the same test can be a good product in a symptomatic or high-risk population and a bad one in the worried well — the market segmentation question for diagnostics companies.
insights.locator: In essence, Bayes tells us how much a new piece of evidence

insights.claim: Isaac Kohane, Daniel Masys and Russ Altman's 'incidentalome' concept showed that a genetic panel equivalent to 10,000 independent tests, each with an extraordinarily good 0.01% false-positive rate, would still leave more than 60% of people tested with at least one false positive.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Multiplex testing breaks even on excellent per-test performance; the more comprehensive the panel a company sells, the worse its aggregate false-positive burden and downstream workup cost.
insights.locator: Their statistical illustration was striking

insights.claim: The proliferation of ever-more comprehensive testing driven by consumer interest in disease pre-emption concerns many physicians including Eric Topol, because looking harder at apparently healthy people risks incidental findings, anxiety, unnecessary workups and occasionally actual harm.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Physician opinion leaders remain a headwind for consumer full-body and full-panel screening businesses — a reimbursement and reputational risk.
insights.locator: This is why the proliferation of ever-more comprehensive testing

insights.claim: The countervailing appeal of comprehensive testing is that most diseases of aging develop gradually over years, potentially offering an opportunity to identify trouble at an earlier and more actionable stage.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: The demand-side rationale that keeps capital flowing into early-detection despite the Bayesian math; it is a real biological argument, not just consumer anxiety.
insights.locator: At the same time, the appeal of such testing

insights.claim: Jacques Balayla at McGill showed mathematically that because Bayesian reasoning is not static — each result becomes the prior for interpreting the next — repeated testing under appropriate assumptions can progressively increase the positive predictive value of a screening result.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Provides the theoretical license for serial-testing business models: the false-positive problem is a property of one-shot testing, not of screening per se.
insights.locator: Rethinking Bayes

insights.claim: The author reversed a long-held position, having for years regarded Bayes primarily as the mathematical explanation for why broad screening of apparently healthy people was so fraught, and now views accumulated context — revealing trajectories over time or complementary signals — as capable of clarifying the picture.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: A credentialed skeptic changing his mind is a sentiment inflection worth tracking for the early-detection and longitudinal-diagnostics sector.
insights.quote: For years, I regarded Bayes primarily as the mathematical explanation for why broad screening of apparently healthy people was so fraught.
insights.locator: But it’s difficult not to feel more hopeful

insights.claim: The core question posed in an npj Digital Medicine Comment by the author with Nathan Price and Dan Sodickson is whether, as serial molecular, imaging and clinical data become easier to collect and AI more capable of integrating them, screening can use individual context rather than evaluating each result largely in isolation against a population reference range.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Frames the shift from population reference ranges to personal baselines — the design principle that separates next-generation diagnostics from panel-selling incumbents.
insights.locator: What Dan, Nathan, and I ask is fairly simple

insights.claim: Dan Sodickson's central claim is that 'False positive rates aren't fixed' — given enough prior context, the interpretive question shifts from whether a finding is abnormal to whether it represents a meaningful new change or simply that individual's baseline.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: If false-positive rates are a function of available context rather than of the assay, then owning a patient's longitudinal data becomes the real diagnostic moat.
insights.locator: Insights from Imaging

insights.claim: In a retrospective single-center analysis of nearly 30,000 patients followed about a decade, AI models predicting current and future risk of clinically significant prostate cancer improved specificity from under 30% with little prior information to more than 90% with richer prior imaging and clinical context, while sensitivity remained around 90%.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: A roughly threefold specificity gain at constant sensitivity is the strongest quantitative case yet for context-aware screening — but it is single-center and retrospective, so external validation is the catalyst to watch.
insights.locator: In a retrospective analysis from his group

insights.claim: Sodickson's group has shown that prior imaging can help reconstruct a subsequent MR image from radically less newly acquired data, supporting an 'Everywhere Scanner' vision of cheaper, more accessible imaging that fills gaps between conventional scans with AI focused on detecting change from an individual's prior image.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Threatens the economics of high-field MRI installed base if interval scans migrate to cheaper, less specialized equipment; Sodickson is now Chief Medical Scientist of Function Health.
insights.locator: There is another potentially important aspect of Dan’s work

insights.claim: A virtuous cycle is plausible in imaging: easier imaging makes serial assessment more practical, serial assessment generates more individual context, and that context makes subsequent imaging both easier to obtain and more informative.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: A genuine compounding-data flywheel — rare in health tech and the mechanism by which an early leader in serial imaging could become structurally hard to displace.
insights.locator: If the approach generalizes, interval scans could eventually

insights.claim: Nathan Price, working with Lee Hood at the Institute for Systems Biology, pioneered 'personal, dense, dynamic data clouds,' initially following 108 generally healthy people with repeated clinical and multi-omic measurements, whole-genome sequencing and activity tracking, reported in a 2017 Nature Biotechnology paper.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Establishes a decade-plus evidence trail behind personal-baseline monitoring, and the people now positioned commercially (Price is CSO of Thorne).
insights.locator: Insights from Molecular Measurement

insights.claim: The Arivale program, an ISB spinout focused on 'scientific wellness,' gathered five years of longitudinal data from nearly 5,000 participants including genomic information, more than 1,000 blood-based measurements, microbiome analyses and Fitbit data, described in a 2021 Nature Communications paper.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: One of the largest existing deep-longitudinal healthy-cohort datasets; its scale is the benchmark any new personal-baseline venture is implicitly competing against.
insights.locator: Across the five year program, nearly 5,000 participants

insights.claim: In a retrospective illustration of three participants who later developed metastatic cancer, one woman's CEACAM5 value remained within the conventional population normal range while having jumped substantially from her own previous measurement and rising further before breast cancer was diagnosed — showing a result can look normal against the population yet be distinctly abnormal for that individual.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Vivid mechanism for why personal-baseline deviation could beat reference ranges, but with n=3 and retrospective design it is a hypothesis generator, not investable evidence.
insights.locator: In a 2025 talk at the Buck

insights.claim: In a Göteborg-2 prostate cancer screening trial analysis, inserting the 4Kscore reflex test — combining kallikrein measurements with clinical information — after an elevated PSA and before MRI would have reduced MRI use by 41%, biopsies by 28% and low-grade cancer diagnoses by 23%, while delaying detection of 4% of clinically significant cancers.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Hard trial-derived numbers showing reflex testing produces large, quantifiable cost and procedure savings — the clearest near-term commercial case in the piece, and a template for payer-facing diagnostics pitches.
insights.locator: Consider prostate-specific antigen, or PSA

insights.claim: The Göteborg-2 4Kscore benefit involves no AI at all — the underlying model uses conventional statistics — so the useful ingredient is additional complementary information rather than algorithmic sophistication.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Deflates the AI premium in diagnostics: the value driver is complementary biological information, which incumbents with conventional models can also capture.
insights.quote: There is no AI magic in that example.
insights.locator: There is no AI magic in that example

insights.claim: Not all trajectories carry information: investigators hoped PSA velocity, the rate of PSA change over time, would improve prediction beyond PSA level itself, but in practice it added surprisingly little independent predictive value.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: The key counterexample against assuming longitudinal data is automatically valuable — trajectory value must be demonstrated per biomarker, not assumed across a platform.
insights.quote: The lesson isn’t that trajectories don’t matter; it’s that some trajectories contain meaningful new information and others largely do not.
insights.locator: There’s a useful counterexample from prostate screening

themes.theme: What AI adds and what must still be proven

insights.claim: Clinicians have always used context but face obvious limits integrating disparate information, so once an individual's relevant context spans years of imaging, hundreds or thousands of molecular measurements, physiological signals and clinical history, interpretation becomes as much a computational problem as a clinical one.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Defines the specific, defensible role for AI in screening — systematic contextual integration at scale — rather than superhuman detection from a single image.
insights.locator: AI and the Future of Screening

insights.claim: Earlier detection matters only if it leads to earlier useful intervention and better health rather than more diagnoses, anxiety and procedures, so context-aware screening must clear the same bar as any medical intervention: prospective evidence that using it leaves patients better off, with cost, overdiagnosis, liability and equity remaining substantial concerns.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: The reimbursement gate: absent prospective outcome data, context-aware screening remains a cash-pay consumer product rather than a covered benefit.
insights.quote: None of this gives comprehensive screening a free pass.
insights.locator: None of this gives comprehensive screening a free pass

insights.claim: The mathematics supports the claim that richer longitudinal context could make screening substantially more informative, but whether it can make patients healthier remains an open empirical question.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Separates the information thesis (well supported) from the outcomes thesis (unproven) — the exact fault line on which early-detection valuations should be discounted.
insights.quote: The task now is to determine whether it can make patients healthier as well.
